In a joint status report released this morning, Apple stated that it is still waiting for Jon Prosser to provide additional documents, and hopes to re-depose Michael Ramacciotti, while both defendants have expressed objections to the way Apple is handling the case. Details below.

According to a joint status report submitted to Judge James Donato, the dispute between Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti over who should be held responsible for delays in the trade secrets lawsuit Apple filed against the two in July 2025 is intensifying.

A little background

As a reminder, shortly after unveiling iOS 26, Apple filed a trade secrets infringement lawsuit against Prosser and Ramacciotti, involving a Prosser video that leaked several system details, including the major visual redesign Liquid Glass that was eventually made public.

Apple alleged that Ramacciotti improperly obtained a development iPhone belonging to an employee, who was subsequently fired over the incident. Ramacciotti then had a FaceTime call with Prosser, showing him unreleased iOS features running on the device.

The case has been contentious since then. Because Prosser failed to respond to Apple's complaint within the deadline, the court clerk entered a default judgment against him (though Prosser has consistently denied ignoring the case).

Eight months later, the court agreed to vacate that default judgment, giving him another opportunity to formally answer the complaint.

Court filings show that Ramacciotti's side did respond to Apple's complaint and has largely cooperated with Apple's discovery requests.

However, since Prosser hired a lawyer and formally joined the litigation, the situation has shifted, with the three parties increasingly at odds over who should bear responsibility for the alleged trade secrets disclosure and the resulting delays.

The latest joint status report

Returning to the latest status report, Apple said it wants Ramacciotti to update his interrogatory responses and submit to another deposition to address what it called "inconsistencies between his testimony and that of Mr. Prosser."

Ramacciotti, however, said he will not agree to another deposition until Apple provides "a roadmap for resolving the claims against him, including what, if anything, Apple still needs from him."

As for Prosser, Apple said it remains "awaiting production of several additional documents requested several months ago, including revenue reports and analytics for his YouTube channel, and communications with third parties referenced in his deposition."

Prosser countered by arguing that "the trade secrets at issue in the case are clearly no longer trade secrets, as they have entered the public domain." In other words, his argument appears to be that because Apple has already released the iOS update containing Liquid Glass, the information at the core of the lawsuit is now publicly available and therefore no longer meets the definition of confidential.

In the joint status report, Ramacciotti asked the court to hold a status hearing this month, during which Apple would have to explain what additional information it still needs from him. He also asked Apple to either drop the claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial within the following 30 days.

Apple, for its part, wants to continue the discovery process, including re-deposing Ramacciotti and pursuing the documents [Prosser] has yet to produce. Prosser, meanwhile, claims he has fulfilled the discovery obligations he agreed to and objects to Apple's continued requests for additional material.

If Judge Donato does not grant Ramacciotti's request for a status hearing, the parties have suggested submitting another joint status report on December 2.
